name: 01_trade_confirmation_matching
raw_text:
Trade Confirmation Matching – Standard Operating
 Procedure
Sample enterprise SOP for workflow-extraction testing
1. Purpose and Scope
This procedure governs the reconciliation of executed trades received from external brokers against trade
records maintained in the firm's internal order management and settlement systems. It applies to standard
listed-equity and similar transactions received through the firm's approved broker communication channels.
The procedure is intended to ensure that a trade is not treated as fully reconciled or settled unless the
essential economic fields in the broker confirmation agree with the firm's internal record.
2. Roles and Responsibilities
The reconciliation service performs the initial comparison of incoming confirmations with internal records.
The operations team is responsible for maintaining the matching rules and monitoring exceptions.
Operations analysts investigate items that cannot be matched automatically. Where an exception cannot be
resolved using the available trade records, the item is escalated according to the existing settlement
operations procedure. The normal matching process does not require an analyst to interpret market
conditions or determine the commercial intent of a trade.
3. Receipt of Confirmation
Broker confirmations are received electronically during the trading day and are placed into the firm's
reconciliation workflow. The incoming record normally contains information identifying the transaction and
the economic terms agreed with the broker. The system validates that the required fields are present before
attempting reconciliation. Records that are incomplete or technically malformed are retained in the existing
exception process rather than being treated as successful matches.
4. Identification of Internal Record
After a valid confirmation is received, the reconciliation service searches the internal order and trade records
for the corresponding transaction. Trade identifiers and other available reference information are used to
identify the expected internal record. If multiple candidate records are returned, the service does not select
one based on subjective interpretation; the item remains unresolved for operational review.
5. Field-Level Reconciliation
For a candidate match, the service compares the security ticker, executed quantity, execution price and
contractual settlement date. The values are evaluated using the configured matching rules. The normal
successful path requires the relevant fields to agree exactly. The system does not use natural-language
interpretation to determine whether two values are economically similar, because the reconciliation control is
designed around explicit field equality.


6. Successful Match
When all required fields satisfy the configured matching criteria, the confirmation is considered reconciled.
The system updates the trade's reconciliation status and allows the existing settlement workflow to proceed.
The matched records remain available in the normal audit trail so that operations personnel can trace the
status update back to the original confirmation and internal trade record.
7. Mismatches and Exceptions
If the quantity, price, settlement date or other required value differs, the trade is not marked as settled
through the automatic path. The system records the mismatch and places the item in the operational
exception queue. Examples include a broker reporting a different executed quantity, a price discrepancy
caused by a correction, or a settlement date that differs from the internal record. The reconciliation service
does not attempt to infer the cause of the discrepancy.
8. Operational Review
An operations analyst reviews exception items using the existing records and procedures. Depending on the
circumstances, the analyst may compare the broker confirmation with the order history, contact the relevant
operations or trading team, or obtain a corrected confirmation. Once the discrepancy has been resolved, the
trade is processed through the established correction and reconciliation procedure.
9. Controls and Auditability
The matching process uses explicit rules and produces a traceable outcome for each confirmation.
Successful matches and unresolved exceptions are recorded separately. Changes to matching criteria are
managed through the firm's existing operational change-control process. The system should not modify a
trade's economic fields simply to achieve a match.
10. Processing Considerations
The process is designed for high-volume repetitive reconciliation. The normal path consists of retrieving a
known record, comparing a fixed set of fields and updating a status when predefined conditions are satisfied.
Human involvement is concentrated on cases where the deterministic comparison fails or the source data is
incomplete.

steps.name: Receive and validate broker confirmation
steps.description: Broker confirmations are received electronically during the trading day and placed into the reconciliation workflow. The system validates that required fields identifying the transaction and its economic terms are present. Incomplete or technically malformed records are retained in the existing exception process rather than treated as successful matches.

steps.description: The reconciliation service searches the internal order and trade records for the corresponding transaction using trade identifiers and other available reference information. If multiple candidate records are returned, the item remains unresolved for operational review rather than being selected based on subjective interpretation.

steps.name: Perform field-level reconciliation
steps.description: For a candidate match, the service compares the security ticker, executed quantity, execution price, and contractual settlement date against the internal record using the configured matching rules. The successful path requires the relevant fields to agree exactly; no natural-language or economic-similarity interpretation is used.

steps.name: Update reconciliation status on successful match
steps.description: When all required fields satisfy the configured matching criteria, the confirmation is considered reconciled. The system updates the trade's reconciliation status, allowing the existing settlement workflow to proceed. Matched records remain available in the audit trail so operations personnel can trace the status update back to the original confirmation and internal trade record.

steps.description: If the quantity, price, settlement date, or other required value differs, the trade is not marked as settled through the automatic path. Items that cannot be resolved using available trade records are escalated according to the existing settlement operations procedure.

steps.description: Once a discrepancy has been resolved, the trade is processed through the established correction and reconciliation procedure. The system does not modify a trade's economic fields simply to achieve a match, and successful matches and unresolved exceptions are recorded separately for auditability.

name: 02_passive_exposure_limit_check
raw_text:
Passive Exposure Limit Check – Daily Portfolio Control
 Procedure
Sample enterprise SOP for workflow-extraction testing
1. Purpose and Scope
This procedure describes the daily control used to identify portfolio holdings or issuer exposures that exceed
limits stated in an applicable investment mandate. It covers the preparation of portfolio data, calculation of
exposure percentages, comparison with configured thresholds and creation of exceptions for positions
outside permitted limits.
2. Source Data
The monitoring process uses the approved portfolio valuation and holdings data for the relevant valuation
point. The required information includes portfolio net asset value, security or issuer-level market values and
the mandate limits applicable to the portfolio. Data is expected to represent a consistent reporting point so
that the resulting exposure percentages are comparable.
3. Portfolio Snapshot
At the beginning of the monitoring cycle, the latest available NAV and holdings snapshot is loaded into the
control process. Data-quality checks confirm that required values are present and that the portfolio can be
evaluated. Where a required source value is unavailable, the issue is handled through the existing
data-quality process rather than being silently substituted with an estimated value.
4. Exposure Calculation
For each relevant holding or issuer grouping, the process calculates the percentage weight relative to
portfolio NAV. The calculated exposure represents the portion of the portfolio attributable to the relevant
security or issuer at the measurement point. The calculation follows the firm's configured methodology and
does not require a subjective assessment of the position.
5. Mandate Limit Application
The applicable investment mandate provides the threshold against which the calculated exposure is
evaluated. Limits are maintained as configured control values where the mandate permits them to be
represented numerically. For example, a single-issuer restriction may specify that exposure must not exceed
five percent of NAV.


6. Threshold Comparison
The control compares each calculated exposure with its applicable limit. A holding at or below the configured
threshold remains within the normal limit for this control, while a holding above the threshold generates an
exception. The comparison is performed consistently across the portfolio without requiring an analyst to
interpret whether a small difference is commercially significant.
7. Exception Creation
For each exceeded threshold, the monitoring process creates an exception record. The record contains
sufficient information for follow-up, including the portfolio, relevant holding or issuer, measured exposure,
permitted limit and observed variance. Exceptions are made available to the monitoring or compliance team
through the established reporting process.
8. Review and Escalation
The daily exposure check is a monitoring control and does not by itself determine the ultimate root cause of
an exception. Where a position is flagged, the relevant team follows the firm's breach investigation
procedure. That investigation may consider additional information that is outside the numerical monitoring
process.
9. Configuration and Change Control
Mandate limits and calculation parameters are maintained under the firm's existing configuration and
change-control procedures. Updates should be traceable to the applicable mandate or approved instruction.
The monitoring process uses the configured values rather than generating or interpreting new limits
dynamically.
10. Operational Characteristics
The control is repetitive and operates on structured numerical data. The core question answered by the
process is whether a calculated exposure exceeds a predefined threshold. The workflow therefore separates
the mechanical identification of exceptions from any subsequent investigation into why an exposure occurred
or whether an exception is ultimately a reportable breach.

steps.name: Load Portfolio Snapshot
steps.description: Load the latest available NAV and holdings snapshot for the relevant valuation point into the control process. Run data-quality checks to confirm required values are present; unavailable source values are handled through the existing data-quality process rather than substituted with estimates.

steps.name: Calculate Exposures
steps.description: For each relevant holding or issuer grouping, calculate the percentage weight relative to portfolio NAV using the firm's configured methodology, representing the portion of the portfolio attributable to the security or issuer at the measurement point.

steps.name: Apply Mandate Limits
steps.description: Retrieve the applicable mandate limits maintained as configured control values (e.g., a single-issuer restriction of no more than five percent of NAV) to serve as the thresholds for evaluation.

steps.name: Compare Exposures to Thresholds
steps.description: Compare each calculated exposure with its applicable configured limit. Holdings at or below the threshold remain within the normal limit; holdings above the threshold generate an exception, applied consistently across the portfolio.

steps.name: Create Exception Records
steps.description: For each exceeded threshold, create an exception record containing the portfolio, relevant holding or issuer, measured exposure, permitted limit, and observed variance. Make exceptions available to the monitoring or compliance team through the established reporting process.

steps.name: Review and Escalate Exceptions
steps.description: For flagged positions, the relevant team follows the firm's breach investigation procedure, which may consider additional information outside the numerical monitoring process to determine root cause and whether the exception is a reportable breach.

name: 03_mandate_breach_root_cause_investigation
raw_text:
Mandate Breach Root-Cause Investigation –
 Compliance Investigation Procedure
Sample enterprise SOP for workflow-extraction testing
1. Purpose and Scope
This procedure describes the investigation performed after a portfolio monitoring control identifies a potential
mandate breach. The objective is to establish whether the alert represents a genuine breach, understand the
circumstances that produced the exposure, identify relevant approvals or exceptions and prepare a
documented conclusion for compliance review.
2. Case Initiation
A new investigation case is opened when an exposure exception is received. The analyst records the
portfolio, security or issuer involved, the reported exposure, the applicable threshold and the time at which
the alert was generated. The initial alert is treated as an investigation trigger rather than as a final
determination of a breach.
3. Mandate Retrieval
The analyst retrieves the investment mandate governing the portfolio and identifies the restriction associated
with the alert. Relevant language may be contained in narrative provisions, schedules, definitions or
supporting documents. The analyst reviews the restriction in context because a numerical alert may not
capture every qualification that affects how the mandate should be applied.
4. Position Evidence
The analyst obtains the holdings snapshot used to generate the alert and, where necessary, retrieves
intraday position information surrounding the reported breach. The purpose is to establish the portfolio's
exposure at relevant points in time and determine whether the reported value accurately reflects the position
during the period under investigation.
5. Transaction History
Historical transactions affecting the relevant security or issuer are reviewed. The analyst considers
purchases, sales, transfers and other recorded activity to understand whether the exposure changed
because of an active portfolio decision or another event. Transaction timestamps are compared with the
timing of the exposure change where this information is available.


6. Exception and Waiver Search
The investigation also checks for pre-approved exceptions, temporary waivers or other documented
permissions that may have applied at the time of the alert. These records may be maintained separately
from the portfolio data and may be stored in documents or case-management records. The analyst verifies
the validity and effective period of any approval identified.
7. Corporate Actions and Passive Movement
The analyst considers whether a corporate action, market movement or another event could have changed
the exposure without a corresponding active investment decision. For example, a change in market value
may cause an exposure percentage to move above a threshold even though no new position was
purchased. The analyst compares the available evidence before reaching a conclusion.
8. Root-Cause Assessment
The evidence is synthesized to determine the most plausible cause of the exception. Possible classifications
include active investment decision, passive market drift, corporate action, operational issue or another
documented circumstance. Where evidence is conflicting or incomplete, the analyst records the uncertainty
and follows the applicable escalation procedure rather than treating an assumption as fact.
9. Genuine Breach or False Positive
After considering the mandate language, position data, transaction history and applicable approvals, the
analyst classifies the alert. A genuine breach is recorded where the evidence supports that the mandate
restriction was actually violated. A false positive is recorded where the alert resulted from an allowable
circumstance, data issue or other condition that means the apparent breach does not represent a reportable
violation.
10. Compliance Write-Up
The analyst prepares a written investigation summary. The document describes the original alert, relevant
mandate provisions, evidence reviewed, root-cause assessment, applicable exceptions or approvals, final
classification and recommended action. The write-up is intended to allow another reviewer to understand
how the conclusion was reached without reconstructing the entire investigation from source systems.
11. Escalation and Human Oversight
Material cases, uncertain interpretations and situations involving incomplete evidence are escalated to the
appropriate compliance or investment oversight personnel. The final regulatory or compliance determination
remains subject to the firm's established governance process. Investigation support does not replace the
responsibility of authorized personnel to approve sensitive conclusions.

name: 04_new_client_onboarding_suitability_review
raw_text:
New Client Onboarding – Suitability Questionnaire
 Review Procedure
Sample enterprise SOP for workflow-extraction testing
1. Purpose and Scope
This procedure governs the review of suitability information submitted during new-client onboarding. The
review considers the client's investment objectives, stated risk tolerance, requested products or strategies
and relevant eligibility or regulatory constraints. The outcome is documented as part of the client's
onboarding record.
2. Client Submission
The client provides a completed risk and suitability questionnaire together with the information requested by
the onboarding process. Responses can include structured selections as well as free-text explanations
describing investment objectives, experience, preferences and circumstances. The onboarding team
associates the submission with the correct client record and makes the available information accessible to
the reviewing function.
3. Completeness Review
The reviewer first checks whether the required information has been provided. Missing responses, unclear
answers or unavailable supporting documents are identified before the suitability assessment is finalized.
Where clarification is necessary, the reviewer follows the firm's established process for requesting additional
information from the client or onboarding team.
4. Investment Objective Assessment
The reviewer considers the client's stated objectives and requested investment approach. The information is
assessed in combination rather than as isolated questionnaire fields. The reviewer considers whether the
requested strategy appears consistent with the objectives and circumstances recorded in the onboarding
materials.
5. Risk Tolerance Assessment
The client's stated risk tolerance is reviewed against the characteristics of the requested investment products
or strategies. The reviewer considers the interaction between the client's responses and the requested
exposure. A conservative risk profile combined with a request for substantial leverage, for example, may
require additional investigation rather than an automatic approval or rejection.


6. Regulatory and Internal Constraints
The reviewer checks applicable regulatory and internal eligibility requirements. Depending on the product,
these may include investor classification, accreditation or other eligibility conditions. The relevant
requirements may be maintained across policy documents, product rules and onboarding procedures,
requiring the reviewer to identify the provisions applicable to the specific case.
7. Inconsistency Identification
Responses are examined for contradictions or combinations that require further attention. Inconsistencies
may arise between risk tolerance and requested leverage, between stated objectives and requested
products, or between client information and supporting documentation. The presence of an inconsistency
does not automatically establish that the client is unsuitable; it creates an issue that must be evaluated and,
where appropriate, clarified.
8. Clarification and Supporting Evidence
Where information is ambiguous or contradictory, the reviewer may request clarification or supporting
evidence. New information is added to the onboarding record and considered alongside the original
responses. The reviewer maintains a clear distinction between information supplied by the client and
conclusions reached during the review.
9. Suitability Determination
After reviewing the available information, the reviewer reaches a suitability determination in accordance with
the firm's policies. The conclusion is based on the applicable requirements and the evidence available in the
case. Situations that fall outside standard guidance are escalated to the appropriate compliance or
supervisory function.
10. Determination Memo
The reviewer prepares a suitability determination memo describing the client's relevant objectives and risk
information, the requested strategy, material constraints or inconsistencies, additional information obtained
and the reasoning supporting the conclusion. The memo is written so that a subsequent reviewer can
understand the basis of the determination.
11. Approval and Record Retention
The completed review is submitted for any required human approval or sign-off. Once approved, the
determination and supporting information are retained with the onboarding record under the firm's
record-management requirements. Material changes to the client's circumstances may require a future
suitability review under the applicable process.

name: 05_quarterly_performance_report_generation
raw_text:
Quarterly Performance Report Generation – Client
 Reporting Procedure
Sample enterprise SOP for workflow-extraction testing
1. Purpose and Scope
This procedure describes the preparation of quarterly portfolio performance reports for client distribution. It
covers the retrieval and validation of performance data, benchmark comparison, controlled disclosure
language, narrative commentary, report assembly and portfolio manager approval.
2. Reporting Period and Data Sources
At the close of each reporting quarter, the reporting team establishes the applicable reporting period and
identifies the approved data sources. Portfolio returns are obtained from the custodian or designated
performance system. Benchmark information is retrieved for the same period and checked against the
benchmark applicable to the portfolio.
3. Data Availability Check
The reporting analyst checks that the required portfolio and benchmark information is available. Missing or
inconsistent records are investigated using the established data-quality process. The report is not finalized
using an unverified value merely because a deadline is approaching.
4. Performance Calculation
Portfolio performance is calculated using the firm's established reporting methodology. The resulting return is
compared with the applicable benchmark return for the same period. Where additional standard metrics are
required by the reporting template, they are calculated using the approved methodology and stored with the
reporting data.
5. Data Review
The calculated figures are reviewed for unexpected changes, missing values or inconsistencies with the
source data. Any issue identified during this review is resolved before the figures are incorporated into the
final client report. The purpose of this review is to ensure that the numerical information presented to the
client is traceable to the approved source.


6. Controlled Disclosure Language
Quarterly reports contain standard risk disclosures and other approved boilerplate language. The reporting
team retrieves the current controlled version of the relevant template or disclosure library. The approved
wording is inserted into the appropriate sections without discretionary rewriting, because changes to
controlled disclosure language may require a separate review and approval process.
7. Portfolio Activity Review
The reporting analyst or portfolio manager reviews material portfolio activity during the quarter. Relevant
purchases, sales, allocation changes and other events are considered together with significant market
developments that affected portfolio results. The purpose is to identify the factors that are genuinely useful
for explaining the quarter to the client.
8. Narrative Performance Commentary
A written narrative is prepared to explain the principal drivers of performance in plain language. The
commentary may need to connect several sources of information, distinguish material drivers from incidental
events and present the explanation in a manner appropriate for the client. The reviewer checks that the
narrative is consistent with the reported figures and portfolio activity.
9. Report Assembly
The report combines the calculated performance figures, benchmark comparison, approved disclosure
language and narrative commentary. The reporting process places each component into the appropriate
section of the standard client-facing template. Formatting checks are performed before the document is
converted to its final PDF form.
10. Quality Review
The completed report is reviewed for numerical consistency, correct benchmark information, completeness
of disclosures and consistency between the narrative and the underlying portfolio activity. Errors identified
during the review are corrected before the report proceeds to final approval.
11. Portfolio Manager Sign-Off
The final report is submitted to the portfolio manager for review and sign-off. The manager considers the
overall presentation, performance commentary and material client-facing statements. If changes are
requested, the report is returned to the reporting team for revision and another review cycle.
12. Distribution and Record
After approval, the report is released through the established client distribution process. The approved
version is retained with the relevant reporting records. The reporting team maintains the source information
and final report so that the client-facing figures and commentary can be traced to the reporting period and
underlying evidence.
